questions.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

options.text: In ss2 I offered english, further mathematics and yoruba.
In SS2 I offered English, Further Mathematics and Yoruba.
In SS2 I offered english, further mathematics and Yoruba.
In ss2 I Offered English, Further Mathematics and Yoruba.

questions.explanation: Names of languages always take a capital letter, since they derive from the names of peoples and places, and the titles of named school subjects are capitalised as well. *SS2* is a class designation written in capitals, and the verb *offered* is an ordinary word that takes none.

distractorRationale.a: Leaves the class level and every subject name in lower case
distractorRationale.c: Capitalises the language but not the subject titles, applying the rule inconsistently
distractorRationale.d: Wrongly capitalises the ordinary verb *Offered* and leaves *ss2* in lower case

questions.stem: Which sentence capitalises the title correctly?

options.text: We were addressed by president Tinubu at the summit.
We were addressed by President Tinubu at the summit.
We were addressed by the President Tinubu at the summit.
We were addressed by the president tinubu at the summit.

questions.explanation: A title takes a capital letter when it comes immediately before a person's name, because it then forms part of that name. Used on its own as a common noun it stays lower case: "the president addressed the summit". Personal names such as *Tinubu* are always capitalised.

distractorRationale.a: Leaves the title in lower case even though it precedes the name
distractorRationale.c: Adds *the* before a title-plus-name combination, which English does not allow
distractorRationale.d: Fails to capitalise both the title and the personal name

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: the hostel belonging to the boys is the
questions.explanation: *Boys* is a plural already ending in -s, so possession is shown by adding an apostrophe after the final s: *boys' hostel*. Writing *boy's hostel* would mean the hostel belongs to a single boy.

distractorRationale.a: Omits the apostrophe altogether, so no possession is shown
distractorRationale.b: Marks singular possession, which changes the meaning to one boy
distractorRationale.d: Adds an extra s to a plural that already ends in s

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: the playground belonging to the children is the
questions.explanation: *Children* is an irregular plural that does not end in -s, so it takes apostrophe plus s just like a singular noun: *children's playground*. The same applies to *men's*, *women's* and *people's*.

distractorRationale.a: Invents the non-existent plural *childrens* and then adds an apostrophe
distractorRationale.c: Uses the invented plural with no apostrophe at all
distractorRationale.d: Omits any possessive marker, leaving two nouns side by side

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The generator has developed a fault in ______ starter motor."
questions.explanation: *Its* is the possessive form and never takes an apostrophe, exactly like *his* and *hers*. *It's* is only ever the contraction of *it is* or *it has*, and substituting the full words here would give "a fault in it is starter motor", which shows immediately that the apostrophe is wrong.

distractorRationale.a: This is the contraction of *it is*, which makes no sense in the sentence
distractorRationale.c: *Its'* is not a form that exists in English
distractorRationale.d: Writing out *it is* produces an ungrammatical sentence

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The candidate ______ script was missing has been asked to report to the office."
questions.explanation: *Whose* shows possession — the script belongs to the candidate — and like *its* it takes no apostrophe. *Who's* is only the contraction of *who is* or *who has*, and expanding it here gives "the candidate who is script was missing", which is clearly wrong.

distractorRationale.a: The contraction of *who is*, which does not fit the possessive sense
distractorRationale.d: The expanded form of the contraction, which produces an ungrammatical sentence

questions.stem: A market signboard reads "Fresh tomatoe's and pepper's for sale". What is wrong with it?

options.text: Nothing; plural nouns take an apostrophe before the s.
An apostrophe must never be used merely to form a plural; it should read "Fresh tomatoes and peppers for sale".
The apostrophes should come after the s, as in "tomatoes' and peppers'".
The nouns should be singular, as in "Fresh tomato and pepper for sale".

questions.explanation: The apostrophe marks possession or omission, never plurality. Ordinary plurals are formed by adding -s or -es with no apostrophe, so the sign should read *tomatoes* and *peppers*. This misuse is so widespread on shop signs that it has been nicknamed the greengrocer's apostrophe.

distractorRationale.a: States the opposite of the rule
distractorRationale.c: Moving the apostrophe still leaves a possessive form where a plain plural is needed
distractorRationale.d: Changing the number does not address the apostrophe error and misstates the goods on sale

questions.stem: The names of the days of the week and the months of the year take capital letters, but the names of the seasons do not.
questions.explanation: True. *Monday*, *Tuesday*, *January* and *December* are proper nouns and take capitals, but *the rainy season*, *harmattan*, *summer* and *winter* are common nouns and stay in lower case unless they begin a sentence or form part of a title.

questions.stem: Ade and Musa jointly own one provision shop. Which form expresses this correctly?
questions.explanation: When two people own one thing jointly, the possessive marker is added only to the second name: *Ade and Musa's shop*. Marking both names, as in option a, would mean they own separate shops.

distractorRationale.a: Marks both names, which signals separate ownership of two different shops
distractorRationale.c: Marks the first name only, which English does not do in either sense
distractorRationale.d: Turns the names into plurals and misplaces the apostrophe

questions.stem: Which sentence applies the capitalisation rules for directions and regions correctly?

options.text: We drove North for two hours and later settled in the north-East.
We drove north for two hours and later settled in the North-East.
We drove north for two hours and later settled in the north-east.
We drove North for two hours and later settled in the North-East.

questions.explanation: A word such as *north* stays in lower case when it names a mere direction of travel, but takes a capital when it names a recognised region, as *the North-East* does in Nigeria. Option b makes exactly that distinction within a single sentence.

distractorRationale.a: Reverses the rule, capitalising the direction and not the region
distractorRationale.c: Leaves the region name in lower case, so the geopolitical zone is not marked
distractorRationale.d: Capitalises the plain direction of travel as well as the region
